Garmin + EMA · Notebook 15 · Development only

Does a longer physiological window help?

A controlled binary logistic comparison of 60 minutes, two hours and six hours—judged by discrimination beyond time and survey context.

3,689 responses · 125 participants · frozen participant folds
01 · Targets02 · Windows03 · Methods04 · Results05 · Detection06 · Controls07 · Recording08 · Selection09 · Next
Six hours did not establish better discrimination than one hour or context. Full six-hour AUROC: 0.508 for Binary A; 0.510 for Binary B. See paired intervals below.
01 / Methods & findings

Two cutoffs, two distinct questions

The three-item composite is unchanged: nervous + (6 − cope) + (6 − control), requiring all three valid 1–5 items. Binary A identifies scores ≥5; Binary B identifies scores ≥10. Neither defines a clinical diagnosis. All 3,706 EMAs remain accounted for; 3,689 valid-score responses from 125 development participants enter every primary comparator.

02 / Methods & findings

A controlled comparison of 60, 120 and 360 minutes

Primary: six hours versus 60 minutes; 120 minutes is secondary. Physiological models all include the same time/survey context. Main training and validation memberships are identical across windows and features. The 47 full single-window candidates exclude earlier-history and adjacent-window columns, even when their names contain that lookback.

Synthetic timeline: minute-resolution actual start 09:22 → cutoff 09:21. The 60-minute window is [08:21,09:21); the six-hour window is [03:21,09:21). Empty minutes stay unobserved. Example item values 4,2,3 yield composite 11: positive in both tasks.

03 / Methods & findings

Nested logistic regression, optimized for ranking

Five unchanged outer participant folds, three grouped inner folds. Tune C={.001,.01,.1,1} and L2/L1/Elastic Net using mean inner AUROC. Refit imputation, scaling, category encoding and selection inside every training split. Balanced and unweighted training are separate experiments. Hard predictions use the fixed 0.5 probability threshold.

Training medians fill feature summaries only. Variable missingness flags are recording-process covariates. Separate controls test correlation filtering, ≥50% training availability filtering, sparse regularization, no flags, missingness-only and quality-only inputs. The 438-feature multiscale sensitivity is not a six-hour model.

04 / Methods & findings

Does six hours add discrimination?

Binary A: full six-hour AUROC 0.508 (0.459–0.557), AP 0.726, balanced accuracy 0.498; versus 60 minutes: ΔAUROC +0.002 (95% interval -0.065 to +0.070), no clear positive difference; versus context: ΔAUROC +0.029 (95% interval -0.043 to +0.101), no clear positive difference. Binary B: full six-hour AUROC 0.510 (0.472–0.546), AP 0.151, balanced accuracy 0.501; versus 60 minutes: ΔAUROC +0.014 (95% interval -0.052 to +0.079), no clear positive difference; versus context: ΔAUROC -0.003 (95% interval -0.046 to +0.038), no clear positive difference.

05 / Methods & findings

Ranking and minority-class detection are different

ROC uses continuous positive-class probability. PR curves must be interpreted beside prevalence; AP is noninterpolated average precision. Binary A's positive class includes both middle and high scores, so its sensitivity is not high-score-only recall. Weighting may change the sensitivity/specificity trade-off without improving ranking.

07 / Methods & findings

Six hours is not six hours of continuous monitoring

Nested source-lineage checks confirm that 2,518 of 3,689 modeled responses gain accepted HR readings between 60 minutes and six hours; 1,171 gain none. The median number added is 1536. This is additional accepted logical records, not additional minutes of continuous monitoring.

Different EMAs can reuse the same sensor records in overlapping windows. These response counts are not independent recording segments, and we do not multiply window counts by six hours to estimate monitoring time.

08 / Methods & findings

Check who complete-case filtering excludes

The common complete-case sensitivity requires the original four HR summaries at all three windows. All its comparators are refitted on identical eligible training and validation responses; other full-block features retain training-only imputation. Native full-feature completeness is reported for coverage, not used to silently discard the primary cohort.

09 / Methods & findings

What this resolves—and what to change next

Does six hours outperform 60 minutes?

Binary A: full six-hour AUROC 0.508 (0.459–0.557), AP 0.726, balanced accuracy 0.498; versus 60 minutes: ΔAUROC +0.002 (95% interval -0.065 to +0.070), no clear positive difference; versus context: ΔAUROC +0.029 (95% interval -0.043 to +0.101), no clear positive difference. Binary B: full six-hour AUROC 0.510 (0.472–0.546), AP 0.151, balanced accuracy 0.501; versus 60 minutes: ΔAUROC +0.014 (95% interval -0.052 to +0.079), no clear positive difference; versus context: ΔAUROC -0.003 (95% interval -0.046 to +0.038), no clear positive difference.

Which cutoff discriminates better?

At the prespecified unweighted full six-hour model, Binary A AUROC is 0.508 and Binary B is 0.510. These are different outcomes, not a clinical cutoff selection. Interpret uncertainty, class support and prevalence alongside the point difference; raw AP is not comparable across prevalence.

Do expanded features add beyond context?

Binary A: ΔAUROC +0.029 (95% interval -0.043 to +0.101). Binary B: ΔAUROC -0.003 (95% interval -0.046 to +0.038). The full model includes recording-missingness flags. A context increment alone does not isolate physiological-value signal; interpret it with no-flags and missingness-only controls, not just F1 or accuracy.

Does feature selection help?

Binary A: sparse versus full: ΔAUROC +0.000 (95% interval +0.000 to +0.000); correlation filter versus full: ΔAUROC +0.003 (95% interval -0.013 to +0.019); availability filter versus full: ΔAUROC +0.000 (95% interval -0.014 to +0.015). Binary B: sparse versus full: ΔAUROC -0.019 (95% interval -0.068 to +0.037); correlation filter versus full: ΔAUROC -0.014 (95% interval -0.063 to +0.041); availability filter versus full: ΔAUROC -0.010 (95% interval -0.061 to +0.047). These are multiple exploratory comparisons; do not select a winning feature set from the outer folds.

Does weighting improve minority detection?

Binary A: balanced sensitivity 0.504 versus 0.993 unweighted; specificity 0.520 versus 0.003; precision 0.730 versus 0.719. ΔAUROC +0.001 (95% interval -0.041 to +0.041). Binary B: balanced sensitivity 0.402 versus 0.004 unweighted; specificity 0.635 versus 0.999; precision 0.152 versus 0.333. ΔAUROC +0.002 (95% interval -0.012 to +0.017). Sensitivity here is for class 1. Binary A's minority is class 0, whose recall is specificity; Binary B's minority is class 1. A changed operating point does not necessarily improve AUROC.

Are recording gaps and missingness affecting performance?

Binary A: missingness-only AUROC 0.447; quality-only 0.467; context 0.479. Removing flags versus full: ΔAUROC +0.007 (95% interval -0.001 to +0.017). Binary B: missingness-only AUROC 0.508; quality-only 0.530; context 0.513. Removing flags versus full: ΔAUROC -0.030 (95% interval -0.082 to +0.030). These controls assess associations with the recording process and handling choices; they cannot establish that gaps caused weak prediction. See per-class missingness and complete-case composition.

What should change next?

Retain strict time-support allowlists, explicit recording indicators and matched-cohort evaluation. Resolve timestamp/batching, sensor quality and prompt/recall evidence. Prespecify confirmation of any promising effect; do not expand the search or open the final test automatically.

These are newly fitted binary, AUROC-tuned logistic experiments. Notebook 12 emphasized macro F1 and different cohorts; Notebook 13's expanded classification and Notebook 14's regression are prior exploratory evidence, not independent confirmation. Their headline metrics are not directly ranked against these results.

Use the prespecified paired full360-versus-full60 and full360-versus-context intervals to assess the primary question. An isolated F1 increase, a large coefficient, or a point maximum does not establish useful physiology. Cutoff comparisons involve different outcomes and prevalence; neither is a validated diagnosis.

Acquisition-versus-receipt timestamps, batching, sensor quality and prompt/recall alignment remain unresolved. Sparse/stale observations and missingness can influence predictions, but these analyses cannot identify their causal contribution. More within-person outcome variation does not guarantee wearable predictability.

Next: preserve a strict single-window feature allowlist; keep recording availability visibly separate; obtain synchronized timing, prompt and quality evidence before automatically expanding features or model searches. Any promising paired effect needs a separately specified confirmation. Keep the final test sealed.
